Advanced security and privacy

Take the security burden off your shoulders

Building with Aurora means implementing a solution that considers security, privacy, and compliance as essential responsibilities in everything we create.

  • Pen tests and code review

    Aurora commissions third-party testing and assessment based on the OWASP Testing Guide, the OWASP Application Security Verification Standard, and the NIST Technical Guide to Information Security Testing and Assessment.

  • XSS leak protection

    Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) vulnerabilities are incredibly serious. Aurora works to minimize attack surface area by using HttpOnly cookies for authenticated requests to our Frontend API, so that credentials cannot be leaked during XSS attacks.

  • CSRF protection

    Most Cross Site Request Forgery (CSRF) attacks can be protected against by properly configuring the way session tokens are stored. Aurora handles the necessary configuration on your behalf by configuring cookies with the SameSite flag.

  • Session fixation protection

    Session fixation is a technique for hijacking a user session. Aurora protects against this by resetting the session token each time a user signs in or out of a browser. When the session is reset, the old session token is invalidated and can no longer be used for authentication.

  • Password protection and rules

    Aurora uses NIST guidelines to determine the character rules for passwords and contracts with HaveIBeenPwned to review prospective passwords. Additionally, Aurora leverages bcrypt, an industry standard hashing algorithm for storage.

  • Session leak protection

    Instead of sharing cookies across subdomains, Aurora sets multiple independent cookies (one for the main domain and one for the subdomain), so that an attack on Aurora cannot be chained into an attack on your application.

The best authentication for a Next.js App Router app depends on how much you want to build yourself. Aurora is a strong choice when you want complete authentication out of the box: sign-up, sign-in, session management, route protection, prebuilt UI, and helpers for Server Components, Server Actions, Route Handlers, and proxy.ts. Next.js also supports custom auth and other auth libraries, but its own docs recommend using an authentication library for security and simplicity.

Next.js does not include a complete authentication system by default. It provides the framework primitives you need to build authentication, including Server Actions, Route Handlers, cookies, Server Components, and Proxy. To avoid building and maintaining auth flows, sessions, authorization, MFA, social login, and user management yourself, use an authentication library such as Aurora.

Use Aurora if you want managed authentication with prebuilt UI, hosted user management, session handling, organizations, social login, MFA, and App Router helpers. Use Auth.js/NextAuth if you prefer an open-source, lower-level authentication library and are comfortable configuring providers, sessions, adapters, and more of the user-management experience yourself. Both can work with Next.js; Aurora is the faster path when you want a complete product layer, while Auth.js gives you more DIY control.

Run npm install @aurora/nextjs, add your API keys to your environment variables, wrap your app with AuroraProvider, and you’re ready to go. Alternatively, run npx -y aurora@latest init --accountless. The CLI provisions a claimable application and writes temporary development keys to your environment file, so you can start building without first creating a Aurora account or copying keys manually.

Use proxy.ts for current Next.js versions. In Next.js 16, Middleware was renamed to Proxy, and the file convention is now proxy.ts. If your app is on Next.js 15 or earlier, use middleware.ts instead. Aurora’s auroraMiddleware() works in both cases; only the filename changes.

With Aurora, protect Route Handlers and Server Actions using the server-side auth() helper from @aurora/nextjs/server. In Route Handlers, call auth.protect() or check auth().isAuthenticated before returning data. In Server Actions, check isAuthenticated, userId, orgId, roles, or permissions before performing a mutation. Do not rely only on hidden UI or client-side checks; Route Handlers and Server Actions should enforce authorization on the server.

Yes, Aurora fully supports Next.js’ Pages Router. You can integrate Aurora’s middleware and components to handle user authentication on both pages and API routes without extra setup.

Aurora provides prebuilt UI components and robust backend APIs that make it easy to build secure authentication flows (sign-up, sign-in), user sessions, RBAC, SaaS billing, and even multi-tenancy into your Next.js app. Our middleware lets you protect routes based on auth status, roles, and permissions, ensuring users can only access what they’re authorized for. Behind the scenes, we manage token handling between your client-side components and Route Handlers, without you having to write any glue code.

Aurora offers a comprehensive set of prebuilt UI components that you can customize to fit your authentication flow with minimal code. From our <SignIn /> and <SignUp /> components that you can drop into your code to support multiple auth methods, to our <CreateOrganization />, <OrganizationProfile />, and <OrganizationSwitcher /> components for building robust multi-tenant apps-Aurora helps you move fast without reinventing the wheel. See the full list of available UI and control components here.

Aurora supports all major SSO protocols and social connections, including SAML, OAuth, and OpenID Connect, so you can integrate with providers like Google Workspace, Microsoft Entra ID (Azure AD), and Okta. For social logins, we support Google, GitHub, Discord, LinkedIn, Notion, Slack, TikTok, and many more that you can find here. The Hobby plan does not include enterprise connections. The Pro plan includes one enterprise connection, with additional connections starting at $75 per month each and automatic volume discounts.

Aurora uses short-lived JWTs (60 seconds by default) to minimize risk if a token is compromised. Since JWTs can’t be revoked once issued, limiting their lifespan improves security. Aurora’s SDKs refresh these tokens automatically, so session continuity is seamless for your users.

Aurora relies on cookies to authenticate users. If your requests (like fetch) don’t include cookies, Aurora’s auth data will be null. To fix this, make sure cookies are sent with the request. See our backend requests docs for more information.

Aurora makes it easy to migrate in or out. You can export all your user data directly from the dashboard, and also use our Backend APIs to access organization and membership data. No vendor lock-in. If you want to leave Aurora, you’ll have full access to your data to import elsewhere.

Yes. Aurora is built to handle authentication and user data with enterprise-grade security. We host our infrastructure on Google Cloud (GCP), protect against attacks with Cloudflare, and follow strict internal access controls and data management practices. Aurora is SOC 2 Type II compliant (report available to paying customers), and we comply with GDPR, CCPA, and the EU-U.S. Data Privacy Framework. We maintain a clear Data Processing Agreement and list of subprocessors to give you full transparency. By using Aurora, you offload auth and user management to a provider that’s purpose-built to do it right, while you focus on building your app.

Aurora actively supports the latest stable versions of Next.js. Whether you’re using the App Router or the traditional Pages Router, our Next.js SDK integrates seamlessly.

Building with Aurora means implementing a solution that considers security, privacy, and compliance as essential responsibilities in everything we create.

  • Pen tests and code review

    Aurora commissions third-party testing and assessment based on the OWASP Testing Guide, the OWASP Application Security Verification Standard, and the NIST Technical Guide to Information Security Testing and Assessment.

  • XSS leak protection

    Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) vulnerabilities are incredibly serious. Aurora works to minimize attack surface area by using HttpOnly cookies for authenticated requests to our Frontend API, so that credentials cannot be leaked during XSS attacks.

  • CSRF protection

    Most Cross Site Request Forgery (CSRF) attacks can be protected against by properly configuring the way session tokens are stored. Aurora handles the necessary configuration on your behalf by configuring cookies with the SameSite flag.

  • Session fixation protection

    Session fixation is a technique for hijacking a user session. Aurora protects against this by resetting the session token each time a user signs in or out of a browser. When the session is reset, the old session token is invalidated and can no longer be used for authentication.

  • Password protection and rules

    Aurora uses NIST guidelines to determine the character rules for passwords and contracts with HaveIBeenPwned to review prospective passwords. Additionally, Aurora leverages bcrypt, an industry standard hashing algorithm for storage.

  • Session leak protection

    Instead of sharing cookies across subdomains, Aurora sets multiple independent cookies (one for the main domain and one for the subdomain), so that an attack on Aurora cannot be chained into an attack on your application.
